records.title: Ship hit by mines

fields.event: (5th Contact) (1st Attack) Lat. 35-45 N. Long. 140-55 E. 8400 ton freighter Sunk by Mines. Sighted a ship approaching from the southward heading almost exactly for this vessel. Ceased laying mines. Intended to permit this vessel to go by and then resume laying mines. Vessel was now identified as a large freighter with a small escort vessel inshore from it. They passed under our stern, this vessel on course 090 at that time. Position could have been perfect for a torpedo attack with stern tubes but considered completion of the mine plant as the immediate objective. A bit over five minutes after the freighter passed our stern, there was a violent explosion.

flags: target sunk by mines during mine laying

records.title: Minefield laid

fields.event: The freighter is 90 degrees from her former course lying in the trough of the seas rolling in the heavy swells violently while the escort vessel is circling her. An excellent view of the freighter was now had. Her back had been broken. Amidships the main deck was awash. About ten feet of the stern was above water and the bow was high out of water. The freighter sank rapidly. She had a raked bow, cruiser or counter stern, composite superstructure, flush deck except for a slight forecastle, one squat stack, masts, etc., not seen. Her appearance was similar to the following Marus: AIKOKU, KINRYU, HIROKAWA, KANSAI, KASII, CANBERRA, KYUSU, SADO, the average tonnage of which is 8400. She was making about 15 knots. The escort vessel appeared to be a motor torpedo boat. The presence of this escort, the first of the vessels sighted off INUBO SAKI with an escort, indicated the high value of the ship. Decided that there would probably be anti-submarine vessels in the vicinity at once so commenced retirement into deep water. We were in fifteen fathoms of water with a considerable distance to go before deep submergence would be possible.

flags: entry continues onto page 4

fields.event: Another violent explosion. Nothing seen. Possibly another mine caught someone, perhaps the escort vessel.

fields.event: 1333(K) (Cont'd) to seaward. Now approximately 6 seaplanes were sighted near NOJIMA SAKI, one of them right over the target. When the target had completeà its turn to head back for port, her main dock forward was awash and her screws were nearly out of water, turning rapidly. It looked as if the one hit would suffice to sink the target. However, the position was nearly perfect for a steri. shot and it was now or never, as the range was opening as the target was hended for port.

records.title: Torpedo attack (narrative)

fields.event: Fired one stern shot at 2500 yards track 100 port. We were positive that the planes would see the wake al.. that there should be anti-submarine vessels here if anywhoro in the Empire. The torpedo hit. The target was woll under by now. The final plunge was not seen but her sinking was nevertheless certain evon without the additional hit. The planes dropped several bombs but no anti-subm rine vossols bothered us. Cleared the area to the southward. The freighter had had a raked bow, counter stern, two shallow wells, one tall slender stack, two combination masts and kingposts. She had dazzlo camouflage. Her appearence was similar to that of the SYOTO MARU (Page 216) of 5139-5426 tons.

records.title: Ship hit by mines

fields.event: (8th Contact) (3rd Attack) Lat. 35-45 N. Long. 140-55 E. 5000 ton freighter Damaged or sunk by mines. The smoke had become four columns of smoke approaching INUBO SAKI. We were approaching for an attack south of INUBO SKI. At this instant, however, the leading ship, which had reached the exact bearing of our mine plants, commenced smoking at least five times as great as before and the three other ships scattered to the northward. The smoke off our mine plants lasted only a few minutes while the other three columns of smoke disappeared to the northward. Consider that a freighter of at least 5000 tons was damaged if not sunk by this mine.

records.title: Torpedo attack (narrative)

fields.event: (10th Contact) (4th Attack) Lat. 34-29 N. Long. 140-38 E. 8500 ton freighter Sunk. Sighted large vessel on a southeasterly course. Commenced approach. The seas had picked up late this afternoon and were now mountainous. Even with 10 feet of periscope out the seas spilled over the sight and the target could be seen only momentarily. Depth control was precarious. Use of high speed, trimming heavy and the excellent performance of duty of the planesmen and the Diving Officer, Lieutenant S. H. GIMBER, U.S.N., were the only reasons why and undetected attack was at all possible. The target was large and zigzagging on courses about 60 degrees apart. She had a cargo of planes on her stern.

flags: "momentarilly" and "why and undetected" typed in source

records.title: Torpedo attack (narrative)

fields.event: Fired 3 bow torpedoes at 700 yard range, 2 hits. The first hit was definitely contact and the second believed to have been influence. In the heavy seas the torpedo depth control must have been uncertain and the target's instantaneous draft likewise. The target immediately took a list to starboard and started down by the bow By sound her screws slowed and then stopped abruptly.

records.title: Torpedo attack (narrative)

fields.event: Fired speed spread of 3 torpedoes at range of 1500 yards 90 port track. Two hits; one hit just under the well deck which folded the forecastle up at an angle of about 45 degrees, and one hit about one-fourth ship's length inside the stern. As soon as we fired we turned at high speed to bring the stern tubes to bear, only one torpedo remaining forward. At this time at least three dozen fishing vessels of various types could be seen approaching the destroyer from shore. The destroyer in the meantime was sinking on an even keel with steam and smoke issuing from her.

records.title: Torpedo attack (narrative)
